extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, writing teachers, and readers interested in craft and narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: A set of practice- and theory-oriented observations about literary craft, audience expectations, and cultural differences in narrative form intended to guide writers and teachers. Emphasizes awareness of plural craft traditions and when to follow or break conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft as expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is a set of expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat craft less as purely aesthetic rules and more as the expectations readers/audiences bring to a work; evaluate choices by how they meet, subvert, or play with those expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations are standardized, not universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations are not universal; they are standardized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conventions emerge from specific communities, institutions, and historical processes rather than from any innate law of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions provide pleasure and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations aren't inherently negative — they provide pleasure and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using conventions can create satisfaction for readers and supply scaffolding for meaning and rhythm; this is a defensible artistic choice, not automatically a compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break conventions to represent authentic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Michelle Cliff rejected standard craft conventions to authentically represent her colonial Jamaican experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate rule-breaking can be necessary to truthfully render particular cultural or historical realities; such deviations should be purposeful and tied to representation rather than mere contrarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft complexity vs. pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is simultaneously more and less complex than typically taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of simplistic craft prescriptions; some aspects are simpler in practice, others are more nuanced than workshop axioms imply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional standardization of craft
rubrics_metrics.description: The Iowa Writers' Workshop promoted craft as non-ideological while spreading individualism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how prestigious programs and institutions canonize certain approaches and present them as neutral, shaping what gets taught and published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Western fiction and individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Western fiction is inseparable from individualism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect Western narrative norms (character focus, interiority, individual agency) to reflect individualist cultural assumptions; consider how those assumptions affect characterization and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question who sets expectations and who may break them
rubrics_metrics.description: Whose expectations guide craft decisions, and who holds the freedom to break those rules?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make deliberate choices about which audience's standards you prioritize and be aware of the power dynamics that permit some writers to transgress conventions while marginalizing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-specific craft expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft expectations belong to specific audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the particular audience(s) you are writing for and shape formal and stylistic choices to align with, challenge, or straddle those audiences' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative craft histories (Kundera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milan Kundera offers alternative craft history emphasizing external forces over individual psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider histories of craft that foreground social, political, and economic forces rather than purely psychological explanations for literary developments when evaluating or teaching form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style/form as apolitical standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Iowa Workshop's focus on style/form served to appear apolitical while standardizing literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that emphasizing 'style' or 'form' can mask ideological shaping of literature; interrogate how formalist stances may still enforce norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare Western and Eastern plot structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Western plot follows Freytag/Aristotle; Eastern uses kishotenketsu (intro, development, twist, reconciliation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting plot, study non-Western structures like kishotenketsu as valid alternatives to conflict-driven arcs; choose structure that suits cultural logic and story aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft as culturally reflective and mutable
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft reflects culture but can evolve to resist and reshape cultural norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use craft not only to mirror dominant cultural values but also intentionally to contest, revise, and participate in cultural change through revision and form choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft requires understanding interpersonal perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding craft means understanding how people perceive each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization and viewpoint should be informed by how social perception functions; empathy and social dynamics are part of craft decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural variation in critical priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese fiction traditions valued structural soundness differently than Western critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect different critical criteria across traditions (e.g., priorities on structure, moral framing, communal vs. individual focus) when evaluating or teaching texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridizing traditions (example: Gish Jen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gish Jen blends Western/Eastern: independent and interdependent selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore hybrids that combine divergent narrative logics and self-conceptions to produce work that speaks across cultural modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Know your audience" fundamentally defines craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify the audience(s) whose expectations you are engaging—this governs voice, structure, disclosure, and rhetorical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple legitimate crafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple legitimate crafts exist; teaching craft as singular is a critical failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting a single canon of 'correct' craft; validate plural practices and instruct students in multiple formal traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masked narrative strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: African American authors employed masked narrative — writing for white and Black audiences simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing from marginalized positions, consider rhetorical strategies that address different audiences at once and the constraints that produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring plots in marginalized narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoptee/marginalized narratives often feature coincidence and reunion plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to thematic and plot patterns common in certain communities; recognize their cultural logic rather than dismissing them as clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules become visible when broken
rubrics_metrics.description: Invisible conventions become visible when broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rule-breaking strategically to reveal assumptions and make readers aware of the conventions that normally operate unnoticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions are debatable
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions remain debatable (e.g., the pathetic fallacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conventions as subjects for critique and discussion rather than immutable laws; justify choices for or against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different worldviews imply different resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Western narrative assumes conflict resolution; alternative worldviews see protagonists as integrated within their world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select endings and character arcs that align with the worldview you intend to represent—resolution may be internal integration rather than conflict triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural context shapes interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural differences shape how audiences perceive narrative events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate divergent readings across cultural contexts and make design choices (detail, pacing, explanatory work) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision as cultural participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft supports particular worldviews; revision enables conscious cultural participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revision not only to polish prose but to tune how your work participates in, reinforces, or resists cultural narratives and values.
